content: Tubal disease is responsible for approximately 20% of infertility cases. Hydrosalpinx, a severe form of tubal disease caused by distal tubal occlusion leading to fluid accumulation in the fallopian tubes, has a particularly detrimental effect on the success rates of assisted reproductive technology (ART). Surgical intervention on the fallopian tubes has been proposed as a potential method to improve ART outcomes in women with hydrosalpinges. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of tubal surgery in women with hydrosalpinges before undergoing in vitro fertilization (IVF) or intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI). A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecology and Fertility Group trials register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, DARE, and two trial registries, as of January 8, 2020. Additional trials were identified through reference checking and consultation with experts in the field. The analysis included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing surgical treatment to no surgical treatment, or comparing different surgical interventions, in women with tubal disease prior to IVF. The primary outcomes assessed were live birth rate (LBR) and surgical complication rate. Secondary outcomes included clinical pregnancy rate (CPR), multiple pregnancy rate, ectopic pregnancy rate, miscarriage rate, and the mean number of oocytes retrieved and embryos obtained. A total of 11 RCTs involving 1,386 participants were included. These trials compared various surgical interventions, such as salpingectomy, tubal occlusion, and transvaginal aspiration of hydrosalpingeal fluid, to no surgery or to each other. None of the studies were assessed as having a low risk of bias across all domains, with limitations including lack of blinding, wide confidence intervals, and small sample sizes. The quality of evidence was rated using the GRADE methodology, and most findings were of very low to low quality, with one moderate-quality result. Salpingectomy versus no tubal surgery: None of the included studies reported on live birth rate for this comparison. The effect of salpingectomy on surgical complications, such as conversion to laparotomy or pelvic infection, is uncertain due to very low-quality evidence (Peto odds ratio [OR] 5.80, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.11 to 303.69; one RCT; n = 204). Salpingectomy likely increases the clinical pregnancy rate compared to no surgery (risk ratio [RR] 2.02, 95% CI 1.44 to 2.82; four RCTs; n = 455; moderate-quality evidence). For women with a baseline CPR of 19% without surgery, the rate with salpingectomy is estimated to range between 27% and 52%. Proximal tubal occlusion versus no surgery: No studies reported on live birth rate or surgical complication rate for this comparison. Tubal occlusion may increase the clinical pregnancy rate compared to no surgery (RR 3.21, 95% CI 1.72 to 5.99; two RCTs; n = 209; low-quality evidence). For women with a baseline CPR of 12% without surgery, the rate with tubal occlusion is estimated to range between 21% and 74%. Transvaginal aspiration of hydrosalpingeal fluid versus no surgery: No studies reported on live birth rate for this comparison. There was insufficient evidence to determine a difference in surgical complication rates between groups (Peto OR not estimable; one RCT; n = 176). It is uncertain whether transvaginal aspiration of hydrosalpingeal fluid increases the clinical pregnancy rate compared to no surgery (RR 1.67, 95% CI 1.10 to 2.55; three RCTs; n = 311; very low-quality evidence). Laparoscopic proximal tubal occlusion versus laparoscopic salpingectomy: The effect of laparoscopic proximal tubal occlusion compared to laparoscopic salpingectomy on live birth rate is uncertain (RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.95; one RCT; n = 165; very low-quality evidence). The effect on clinical pregnancy rate is also uncertain (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.07; three RCTs; n = 347; very low-quality evidence). No studies reported on surgical complication rates for this comparison. Transvaginal aspiration of hydrosalpingeal fluid versus laparoscopic salpingectomy: No studies reported on live birth rate for this comparison. There was insufficient evidence to determine a difference in surgical complication rates between groups (Peto OR not estimable; one RCT; n = 160). The effect of transvaginal aspiration of hydrosalpingeal fluid compared to laparoscopic salpingectomy on clinical pregnancy rate is uncertain (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.07; one RCT; n = 160; very low-quality evidence). Conclusions: Moderate-quality evidence suggests that salpingectomy prior to ART likely improves the clinical pregnancy rate compared to no surgery in women with hydrosalpinges. Low-quality evidence indicates that tubal occlusion may also increase the clinical pregnancy rate compared to no intervention. However, there is insufficient evidence to determine the impact of tubal surgery on procedureor pregnancy-related adverse events. None of the studies reported on long-term fertility outcomes. Further high-quality trials are needed to clarify the effects of tubal surgery on live birth rates, surgical complications, and the relative efficacy and safety of different surgical approaches in women with hydrosalpinges undergoing ART.
